levels.title: Island Census
levels.story: The Bridge Isles are scattered across the water, and the council has no map of who is linked to whom. Kit draws one, island by island, and learns the words for what it sees.

everyday.scene: A friend group chat: some people know each other, some only know one person, and one friend does not know anyone else in the group.
everyday.question: How would you draw who knows whom, and how would you store it in a computer?
everyday.answer: Dots for people and lines for friendships. That drawing is called a graph, and it is the basic picture behind maps, social networks and the internet.

lessons.title: Dots and lines
text: A graph is a set of vertices (the dots) joined by edges (the lines). Here the islands are vertices and the bridges are edges. The degree of a vertex is how many edges touch it. A path is a walk along edges from one vertex to another.

A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices. A cycle is a path that starts and ends at the same vertex without reusing an edge. A graph that falls into separate pieces has several connected components.

terms.meaning: A line joining two vertices. Here, a bridge.
The number of edges at a vertex.
A group of vertices that can all reach each other.

predict.prompt: A graph has 3 separate groups of islands. How many connected components?

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 5: Basic Graph Algorithms

lessons.title: Counting bridges
text: Each bridge has two ends, so it adds 1 to the degree of two islands. So the degrees always add up to twice the number of edges. On our map: A=2, B=2, C=3, D=1, E=0, F=1, H=1, which adds to 10, and the map has 5 bridges.
The number of connected components is 3: the group A, B, C, D, then E on its own, and F with H. An island with no bridges is a component of its own.

predict.prompt: A map has 12 bridges. What do the degrees add up to?
predict.answer: 24. Every bridge is counted at both ends.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 5: Basic Graph Algorithms

lessons.title: Storing a graph
text: A computer can store a graph two ways. An adjacency matrix is a square grid with one row and column per vertex, with a mark where two vertices are joined. For 7 islands that is 49 cells. An adjacency list gives each vertex a list of its neighbours.

For an undirected graph the lists hold 10 entries in total, which is twice the edges. When most vertices have few neighbours, lists use far less space. A matrix gives a quick answer to "are these two joined?", at the cost of V × V space.

terms.meaning: A V × V grid showing which pairs are joined.
For each vertex, a list of its neighbours.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 5: Basic Graph Algorithms

fieldNotes.title: Graphs are everywhere
fieldNotes.text: Road maps, friend networks, the links between web pages and the cables between routers can all be drawn as graphs. Once you see them that way, one set of methods works for all of them.

summary: You learned the words vertex, edge, degree, path, cycle and connected component, counted degrees, and compared a matrix with an adjacency list.
The council has its map. "Now we can ask questions of it," says the mayor. Next, Kit walks it.

mistake.title: Forgetting that a lone island is a component
mistake.text: An island with no bridges is its own connected component, so it counts toward the number of groups.

levels.title: Deep Dive
levels.story: Kit has a map and a lantern. The mayor wants to know which islands can be reached from the first one, and the quickest way is to go as deep as possible down one route before trying another.

everyday.scene: You are in a maze with a ball of string. You walk down a corridor to the end. If it is a dead end, you follow the string back to the last junction and try another corridor.
everyday.question: What would you need to remember to do this?
everyday.answer: The path you took, so you can back up. That is depth-first search: go deep, and back up when stuck.

lessons.title: Go deep, then back up
text: Depth-first search (DFS) starts at one vertex and marks it seen. Then it picks any neighbour not yet seen, moves there, and does the same. When a vertex has no unseen neighbours, it backs up to the vertex before and tries its next neighbour.
Marking vertices as seen means no island is visited twice, even if the graph has cycles. With neighbours taken in alphabetical order, DFS from A on our map visits: A, B, D, H, E, F, C.

terms.meaning: Explore as deep as possible, then back up.
Marked as already seen, so it is not visited twice.

predict.prompt: DFS reaches an island with no unseen neighbours. What does it do?
predict.answer: It backs up to the previous island.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 6: Depth-First Search

lessons.title: The path is a stack
text: To back up, DFS must remember the path. The path works like a stack: you push an island when you arrive, and pop it when you back up. A stack gives out the most recently added thing first, like a pile of plates.
A recursive method gets this for free, because the computer keeps the calls waiting like a stack. Either way, the most recent island is the first one to be revisited when you back up.

terms.meaning: Last in, first out: the newest item is taken first.

predict.prompt: A stack holds A, B, D (D on top). You back up. Which island is on top?

lessons.title: What DFS is good for
text: DFS visits every island reachable from the start, and looks at each bridge from both ends, so on our map 16 bridge-looks for 8 bridges. Its work grows with the number of vertices plus the number of edges.
It can find all connected components, tell whether a graph has a cycle, and help build a topological order. It does not find the shortest path: the first route it finds may be a long way round.

predict.prompt: Does DFS find the route with the fewest bridges?
predict.answer: Not necessarily. It takes the first route it finds going deep.

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 6: Depth-First Search

fieldNotes.title: Mazes and file folders
fieldNotes.text: Exploring a folder, with its folders inside folders, is naturally depth-first: open one folder, dive into it, and come back out. Solving mazes with a trail behind you is the same idea.

summary: You watched depth-first search dive and back up, saw that a stack remembers the path, and counted its bridge-looks as twice the number of bridges.
The mayor tips the lantern. "So every island on the map is reachable from the first." But not by the shortest route, so a different explorer is coming.

mistake.title: Forgetting to mark islands visited
mistake.text: Without marking, DFS on a graph with a cycle walks round and round forever. Mark an island the moment you arrive.

levels.title: Ripple Out
levels.story: A stone dropped in water makes rings. Ferry Master Fen wants to know how many bridges stand between the harbour and every other island, and the answer spreads out in rings too.

everyday.scene: You post a rumour to your friends. Next day, their friends have heard it. The day after, their friends' friends have too.
everyday.question: How many days until it reaches a particular person?
everyday.answer: The number of friendships on the shortest chain between you. Breadth-first search finds exactly that, ring by ring.

lessons.title: Ring by ring
text: Breadth-first search (BFS) visits the start, then every island one bridge away, then every island two bridges away, and so on. Like ripples, it finishes each ring before starting the next.

It uses a queue: a line where the first one in is the first one out. Take an island from the front, add its unseen neighbours to the back, and repeat until the queue is empty. Marking islands as seen when they join the queue stops repeats.

terms.meaning: Visit everything near first, then further out, ring by ring.
First in, first out, like a line at a shop.

predict.prompt: A queue holds B, C, D (B at the front). Which is taken next?

lessons.title: The fewest bridges
text: When all bridges count the same, BFS finds the fewest bridges to every island. An island discovered in ring k has distance k, and no shorter route exists, because every closer island was handled in an earlier ring.
On our map, distances from A are A = 0, B = 1, C = 1, D = 2, E = 2, F = 2, H = 3. The farthest island is H, 3 bridges away.

predict.prompt: Island X is in ring 3. How many bridges is the shortest route?

references.title: Algorithms, by Jeff Erickson, chapter 5: Basic Graph Algorithms

lessons.title: What BFS costs
text: Each island enters the queue once, and each bridge is looked at from both of its ends. So the work grows with the number of islands plus the number of bridges, the same as DFS.

The difference is memory and meaning. DFS only holds the current path. BFS may hold a whole ring in the queue, which can be large. In return, BFS gives you shortest routes when every bridge counts the same.

predict.prompt: Which can use more memory on a wide graph: DFS or BFS?
predict.answer: BFS, because it may hold a whole ring in the queue.

deeper.title: Weighted bridges
text: If bridges have different lengths, BFS no longer finds the shortest route. Other methods handle that.

fieldNotes.title: Friends of friends
fieldNotes.text: Ring-by-ring search suits questions like "who is within two steps of me?". Everyone one step away is the first ring, and everyone two steps away is the second. A friend-suggestion feature could use it.

summary: You watched BFS spread in rings, used a queue, and read the fewest-bridge distances straight off the ring numbers.
Fen draws the rings on the chart. "Two bridges from the harbour, no more." Next, Kit puts both explorers on one map.

mistake.title: Marking an island seen only when it is taken from the queue
mistake.text: Mark it when it joins the queue. Otherwise it can be added several times by different neighbours.

levels.title: Same Map, Two Explorers
levels.story: Two explorers, Dive and Ripple, start from the same island on the same map. They both visit every island, but in different orders and for different reasons. Kit compares their notes.

everyday.scene: Two friends search a big shop for a lost phone. One walks every aisle to the end and back. The other checks every aisle entrance first, then every aisle midpoint.
everyday.question: Both find the phone. Which would you pick if the phone is probably near the entrance?
everyday.answer: The second, because it checks nearby places first. Which search to use depends on what you want to know.

lessons.title: Same map, two orders
text: On our map from A, DFS visits A, B, D, H, E, F, C. BFS visits A, B, C, D, E, F, H. Both visit all 7 islands exactly once, but they put them in a different order.

DFS is the stack explorer. It dives, and its order follows one long route at a time. BFS is the queue explorer. It spreads, and its order follows distance from the start. The only difference in the method is stack versus queue.

predict.prompt: What single change turns DFS into BFS?
predict.answer: Using a queue instead of a stack.

lessons.title: The same cost
text: With adjacency lists, both methods touch each island once and each bridge twice, so both take about V + E steps. Neither is faster than the other in this sense. The choice is about the answer you want.
With an adjacency matrix, finding an island's neighbours means scanning a whole row. For V islands that is V × V cells in total, which is slow when most cells are empty.

predict.prompt: Two graph searches both take about V + E steps. How do you choose?
predict.answer: By what you need: shortest routes, or deep exploration, or the memory available.

lessons.title: Which to choose
text: Choose BFS for the fewest bridges, for everything within a given distance, or for spreading in rings. Choose DFS for finding cycles, for listing every component, for topological order, and when the graph is deep rather than wide.
Both answer 'is there a route from here to there at all?', and both find connected components. Then pick the simpler one. Many programs write DFS with recursion in a few lines.

predict.prompt: You need all islands within 2 bridges of the harbour. DFS or BFS?
predict.answer: BFS: it already works in rings.

feed.prompt: You need the fewest bridges from the harbour to every island. Which search?
feed.explain: BFS works in rings of distance.

feed.prompt: With adjacency lists, about how many steps do DFS and BFS take?
feed.answer: About V + E: each island once and each bridge twice.

feed.prompt: DFS is often used to find cycles because...

options.text: Reaching an already visited island by a new bridge shows a loop

feed.explain: Two routes meeting show a cycle.

fieldNotes.title: Pick the search by the question
fieldNotes.text: Ring-by-ring search finds a route with the fewest steps when every step counts the same, such as a simple map of links. Dive-and-back-up search can put tasks into an order that respects what must come first (a topological order).

summary: You put both explorers on one map, saw that DFS and BFS visit the same islands in different orders, and matched jobs to the right one.
The mayor files both reports. "Two tools, one map." The Bridge Isles are charted.

mistake.title: Thinking one search is always better
mistake.text: Both take about V + E steps with adjacency lists. The right one depends on whether you need distances (BFS) or a deep exploration (DFS).
